pages.name: Real and reactive
pages.task: These two sets will share a load of kW and kVAr. A load takes 100 kVA at 0.8 power factor. How many kW does it take?
pages.why: 100 × 0.8 = 80 kW. The other part is √(100² − 80²) = 60 kVAr. That is the reactive power the field supplies.

pages.name: More fuel, wider angle
pages.text: On a live board, a set's rotor is locked in step with the others. So more fuel cannot simply speed it up. Instead it pushes the rotor a few degrees further ahead. The load angle δ grows, and the set sends out more kW. Here the load comes on, and each governor adds fuel as the board slows. A set's kW follows its engine's output. At 600 kW, A carries 300 kW at a δ of 18.5°.

pages.name: Power from the angle
pages.task: Set A's E is 2.25 per unit, V is 1.0 and Xs is 1.5. The load angle is 32.3°. Power = E × V × sin δ ÷ Xs. What power does it send out, in per unit?
pages.why: 2.25 × 1.0 × 0.534 ÷ 1.5 = 0.80 per unit. On a 630 kVA set that is 504 kW. That is its full rating.

pages.name: Two droop lines
pages.text: Two sets share the load through their droop lines. Each runs at 62.4 Hz with no load and 60 Hz at its full 504 kW. So each takes 210 kW for each hertz it falls. A's line starts at the left edge and B's at the right. The 600 kW load lies between. Both run at the board's one frequency, so they settle where the lines cross. That gives 300 kW each, at 62.4 − 300 ÷ 210 = 60.97 Hz. Lowering both settings together would bring the board back to 60 Hz.

pages.name: A nudge to A
pages.task: You raise A's governor setting by 0.3 Hz, from 62.4 to 62.7 Hz. What happens?
pages.answer: A takes more kW, B less, and the frequency rises a little
pages.why: A's line lifts, and the crossing moves towards B. The board can have only one frequency. So the two shares change instead.

pages.name: Half the nudge
pages.text: A's extra fuel starts to push the board faster. B's governor sees the rise and backs off its fuel. They settle with A on 331.5 kW and B on 268.5 kW. A's load angle has grown to 20.5°. The board rose only 0.15 Hz. That is half the nudge. On a set alone, the same nudge would lift the frequency the full 0.3 Hz. It would move no kW. In a big group, the frequency hardly moves at all.

pages.name: Unequal droops
pages.task: A has a 2% droop and B 4%. Each reaches 60 Hz at its full 504 kW. At 900 kW, A carries 432 kW and B 468 kW. The load falls to 300 kW. What happens to the shares?
pages.answer: A sheds twice as much as B, so the shares drift apart
pages.why: As the load falls, the board rises. A gives up 420 kW for each hertz and B only 210. So A sheds 400 kW and B 200. A ends on 32 kW and B on 268 kW. So every set needs the same droop, or the shares drift apart each time the load changes.[^5]

pages.name: Two flat lines
pages.task: Both governors are isochronous, with no droop. A is set to 60.1 Hz and B to 60.0 Hz. They share a 400 kW load. What happens?
pages.answer: A takes it all, and B is driven as a motor
pages.why: A adds fuel until the board runs at 60.1 Hz. B sees the board above its setting and cuts its fuel to nothing. B's rotor is still locked in step, so the board drives it as a motor. Take its draw as an example 50.4 kW. Then A carries 400 + 50.4 = 450.4 kW.

pages.name: Voltage and kVAr
pages.text: Now the picture shows voltage against kVAr. The same 600 kW load at 0.8 also takes 450 kVAr. The AVRs share that kVAr, just as the governors share the kW. Here each AVR lets its voltage fall 1 V for every 30 kVAr it carries. This gentle fall is voltage droop. At a full 630 kVAr it comes to 21 V, or 4.8%. That is close to a common factory setting of 5%. Both are set to 447.5 V at no kVAr. So the lines cross at 440 V, with 225 kVAr each.

pages.name: More field on A
pages.task: Both sets carry 300 kW and 225 kVAr at 440 V. You raise A's field setting by 2 V. What happens?
pages.answer: A's kVAr goes up and its power factor down
pages.why: The board rises only 1 V, to 441 V. A sits 8.5 V below its setting. So it carries 30 × 8.5 = 255 kVAr. B carries 195 kVAr. A's kW stays at 300 kW. So its power factor falls.[^3]

pages.name: Cross current
pages.text: A's kW has not moved. But A now carries 255 kVAr and B 195. Each carries its fair 225 kVAr, plus or minus 30 kVAr. That 30 kVAr runs round from A into B, not to the load. It is a cross current. Here it is 30 000 ÷ (√3 × 440) = 39.4 A. It adds to A's current and its heating. Cross-current compensation cures it. The AVRs compare their kVAr and trim their fields until it matches. The cross current falls to zero.

pages.name: The neutrals
pages.text: Paralleled sets have a third path for current, through their neutrals. Many windings make a small third harmonic, in step in all three phases. So these add in the neutral. If two sets' windings differ, a large current can run round through their star points. A 2/3 pitch winding makes no third harmonic, so it suits paralleling. Where neutrals are earthed, only one running set's is earthed at a time. On an insulated system, coupling two boards couples their insulation monitors too. Only one may stay on.
